Reducing heating costs in an apartment building typically requires a combination of envelope improvements, system optimizations and behavioral measures. Even without specific property data, the following strategies are broadly applicable:

1. Conduct an Energy Audit or EPC Review  
   • Engage a qualified energy consultant to carry out a detailed audit or review the building’s latest Energy Performance Certificate (EPC).  
   • Identify the biggest heat losses (e.g. poorly insulated walls, ceilings or windows) and rank potential measures by cost-effectiveness.

2. Improve Building Envelope  
   • Insulation – Add or upgrade insulation in lofts/attics, external walls (external or cavity insulation) and basement/slab edges.  
   • High-performance windows – Replace single- or old double-glazed windows with low-U-value glazing (e.g. triple glazing or coated double glazing).  
   • Seal air leaks – Apply weather-stripping around doors and windows, seal gaps around pipe penetrations and roof eaves.

3. Optimize the Heating System  
   • Balance radiators or heat emitters – Ensure each radiator or underfloor circuit receives the correct flow to avoid overheating in some apartments and under-heating in others.  
   • Install thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs) – Gives residents individual temperature control, preventing wasteful overheating.  
   • Upgrade boiler or heat pump – Replace an old, inefficient boiler with a modern condensing gas boiler or a ground/air-source heat pump suited to the building’s heat demand.  
   • Regular maintenance – Service boilers, purge air from radiators and check pump performance annually to maintain optimum efficiency.

4. Implement Smart Controls  
   • Building-wide control system – Use a weather-compensated or demand-controlled central heating controller that adjusts flow temperatures based on outdoor conditions.  
   • Zoned heating schedules – Program heating to lower setpoints during unoccupied periods (night, work hours) and raise them before peak occupancy.  
   • Remote monitoring – Install submeters and smart thermostats so managers can identify unusual consumption and intervene early.

5. Recover and Reuse Heat  
   • Heat-recovery ventilation (HRV) – Recover heat from exhaust air in common corridors or apartments and use it to pre-heat incoming fresh air.  
   • Condensing on-site equipment – If the building has an internal CHP (combined heat and power) plant, ensure it operates in condensing mode when return‐water temperatures are low.

6. Engage Residents  
   • Education and feedback – Provide simple guidelines on thermostat settings (e.g. 20 °C in living rooms, 18 °C in bedrooms), window-ventilation practices and radiator operation.  
   • Billing transparency – Use consumption-based heat billing (e.g. individual heat allocators or sub-meters) to encourage responsible use.

7. Explore Renewable and District Solutions  
   • Solar thermal panels – Pre-heat domestic hot water or supplement space heating if roof orientation and budget allow.  
   • District heating – If district heat is available in your area, evaluate whether switching from individual boilers to a district system yields cost or carbon savings.

By combining building envelope upgrades, modern heating technology, smart controls and resident engagement you can significantly lower heat demand and operating costs. A phased approach—starting with a professional energy audit—will help you prioritize measures for the greatest return on investment.

An energy declaration (energideklaration) provides a building board with a clear, standardized snapshot of the building’s current energy performance and concrete advice on how to improve it.  Typically it includes:

• Energy performance class (epc_egienergiklass)  
  – A grade from A to G showing how efficient the building is, relative to national benchmarks.  

• Annual energy use  
  – Total and specific consumption (kWh/year and kWh/m²·year), broken down by heating, domestic hot water, ventilation, cooling, etc.  

• Building characteristics  
  – Heated floor area (Atemp) (epc_egenatemp)  
  – Number of above-ground floors (epc_egenantalplan)  
  – Number of stairwells (epc_egenantaltrapphus)  
  – Building type (apartment block, detached house, etc.) (epc_egenbyggnadstyp)  
  – Owner-built flag (if relevant) (epc_egennybyggar)  

• Technical information  
  – Construction details of walls, roof, windows and doors  
  – Type and efficiency of heating, ventilation and cooling systems  

• Improvement recommendations  
  – A prioritized list of energy-saving measures (insulation upgrades, window replacement, heat-recovery ventilation, etc.), with estimated investment costs and expected energy and CO₂ savings  

• Certificate validity and identification  
  – EPC ID, issue date and the auditor’s credentials, ensuring traceability and compliance with Swedish regulations  

For a building board, this declaration is the basis for budget planning, long-term maintenance strategies and decisions about energy-efficiency investments, helping to reduce both operating costs and environmental impact.

To reduce your building’s heating costs most effectively, you should prioritize measures that improve its overall energy performance as reflected by its EPC energy class (epc_egienergiklass). Even without specific values, the following steps will generally yield the greatest savings:

1. Verify and Improve Your Energy Class  
   • Obtain the latest EPC (energideklaration) for your building and note the epc_egienergiklass.  
   • Target upgrades that move you at least one class higher (for example, from class E to class D), since each step up typically corresponds to 5–10 percent lower annual heating demand.

2. Enhance Building Envelope Insulation  
   • Roof and Attic: Add or upgrade insulation to reduce heat loss through the top of the building.  
   • External Walls: Insulate from inside or outside, depending on façade constraints.   
   • Ground Floor/Floor Slab: Insulate against cold ground to cut conduction losses.

3. Upgrade Windows and Doors  
   • Install high-performance glazing (e.g. triple-glazed windows with low-E coatings).  
   • Ensure tight seals around frames to eliminate drafts.  

4. Improve Airtightness and Ventilation  
   • Air-seal cracks, service penetrations and junctions. A blower-door test can identify major leaks.  
   • Install or upgrade mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR) to maintain fresh air without dumping heat.

5. Optimize Heating System Efficiency  
   • Replace old boilers with high-efficiency condensing boilers or ground/air-source heat pumps.  
   • Add thermostatic radiator valves (TRVs) and smart thermostats to zone-control temperatures by area.  
   • Balance and purge radiators or under-floor circuits to ensure even distribution of heat.

6. Right-size and Control Based on Heated Area (Atemp)  
   • Verify your EPC’s reported Atemp (epc_egenatemp) to ensure your heating system is neither overspecified nor undersized.  
   • More floors or stairwells (epc_egenantalplan, epc_egenantaltrapphus) may require zoned controls.

7. Monitor and Adjust  
   • Install energy meters or smart heat cost allocators to track real-time consumption.  
   • Use the data to fine-tune set-points and identify unusual losses.

By systematically strengthening the building envelope, upgrading the heating plant, and fine-tuning controls, you’ll move to a better EPC class and realize lower heating bills year after year.

When you have no specific data to go on, it’s best to follow a broadly accepted hierarchy of building-performance priorities. In most cases you should:

1. Energy Performance  
   • Aim to improve your EPC energy class (the higher the class, the lower your energy use and operating costs).  
   • Typical high-impact measures: upgrading insulation (walls, roof, ground floor), improving air-tightness, installing energy-efficient windows and doors, and adding heat-recovery ventilation.  
   • Consider low-carbon heating (e.g. heat pumps) and on-site renewables (solar PV) as next steps.

2. Regulatory Compliance & Safety  
   • Verify that you meet all current Swedish Building Regulations (BBR) – fire safety, structural load requirements and accessibility rules (entrances, lifts, corridors).  
   • Ensure all installations (electrical, gas, HVAC) are certified and periodically inspected.

3. Indoor Environmental Quality  
   • Provide adequate fresh-air ventilation and filtration, control humidity to avoid mould, and optimize daylight and glare.  
   • Sound insulation between apartments or office spaces is often mandated by BBR and greatly improves occupant comfort.

4. Maintenance & Life-Cycle Planning  
   • Establish a preventive maintenance plan for façades, roofs, mechanical systems and safety equipment (alarms, sprinklers, lifts).  
   • Budget for periodic overhauls or component replacements to avoid unplanned downtime or costly emergency repairs.

5. Digitalization & Monitoring  
   • Install sensors and metering (electricity, heat, indoor climate) so you can track performance in real time.  
   • Use the data to fine-tune operations, spot faults early and plan future upgrades based on actual consumption patterns.

If you already have an EPC, start by targeting the measures that deliver the greatest energy savings per investment krona. Once you’ve secured a strong energy class, you can channel extra resources into enhanced comfort, renewables or smart-building functions.

Direct-acting (also called “instantaneous” or “direct-conversion”) electric radiators convert virtually all incoming electricity into heat at the point of use – in that sense their “terminal” efficiency is effectively 100 %. However, when evaluating true energy efficiency you must distinguish between:

1. Point-of-use efficiency  
   • 100 % of the electrical energy is converted to heat in the radiator.  
   • There are no flue losses, combustion losses or fuel-storage losses.

2. Primary-energy efficiency  
   • Electricity production, transmission and distribution incur losses (typically 30–40 % or more depending on generation mix).  
   • If your grid mix is based on fossil fuels, the carbon footprint and primary-energy factor are comparatively high.

3. Operational cost and EPC impact  
   • Running costs for direct-acting electric heating are generally higher than for heat pumps or district heating.  
   • In most national energy performance certificates (EPCs), electrical resistance heating tends to give a lower (worse) primary-energy score and thus can negatively affect the building’s overall EPC energy class (epc_egienergiklass).

4. When they can make sense  
   • As a supplemental or spot-heating solution (e.g. infrequently used rooms, holiday homes).  
   • In regions with very clean (renewable) electricity where the primary-energy and carbon penalties are minimal.  
   • Where upfront investment must be kept low and no other heating infrastructure exists.

5. More efficient alternatives  
   • Air-source or ground-source heat pumps (coefficients of performance of 3–5, i.e. 300–500 % point-of-use efficiency).  
   • District heating, biomass boilers or solar-thermal systems, where available.

Conclusion  
Direct-acting electric radiators are 100 % efficient at converting electricity into heat in the room, but because of the upstream losses in power generation and grid distribution, they are generally not considered an energy-efficient primary heating solution and usually result in a lower EPC energy class compared with heat pumps or district heating.

Here are several practical strategies to get the most out of direct-acting electric radiators—both in terms of comfort and running costs:

1. Fit Programmable Controls  
   • Use a weekly timer or smart thermostat to switch your radiators on only when you need them (for example, 1–2 hours before you get up and after you return home).  
   • Lower the set‐back temperature by a few degrees during the night or when the house is empty; each degree of setback can save around 5 % in energy.

2. Install Thermostatic Radiator Valves (TRVs)  
   • TRVs allow you to set each radiator to a different temperature—ideal for rooms you use less (bedrooms, guest rooms) versus living areas.  
   • They maintain a constant target temperature by cycling the element on and off at that radiator only.

3. Improve Fabric Efficiency  
   • Seal drafts around windows and doors with weather‐stripping or draft excluders.  
   • Add insulation where possible—especially loft insulation to cut heat loss to unheated roof spaces.  
   • Consider secondary glazing or heavy thermal curtains to reduce cold surfaces.  

4. Positioning and Airflow  
   • Keep radiators clear of furniture, curtains or towels so that warm air can circulate freely.  
   • Fit foil-backed radiator reflectors between radiators and external walls to reflect heat back into the room.  
   • Use small radiator fans or “air amplifiers” at the top of the unit to help distribute warm air faster.

5. Zone Heating and Door Management  
   • Close doors to rooms you don’t use regularly—and turn those radiators down to frost‐protect settings (around 5 °C).  
   • Group radiators on separate circuits or channels in your control system so you’re not overheating unused spaces.

6. Use Off-Peak Electricity Tariffs  
   • If your supplier offers Economy 7/Economy 10 or a similar night‐rate tariff, program your heaters to warm up during low-price hours where feasible (but beware of over-heating and storing too much heat).

7. Regular Maintenance  
   • Wipe dust off the radiator and vents periodically—dust can insulate the element and reduce its output.  
   • Check that wiring and thermostats are in good order; ageing controls can introduce temperature overshoots.

8. Fine-Tune Set Temperatures  
   • Aim for around 20 °C in living areas and 16–18 °C in bedrooms.  
   • Experiment with lowering the thermostat by 1 °C—most people won’t notice a small drop in temperature, but it can yield 5–10 % savings.

By combining good control, zoning, building envelope improvements and regular upkeep, you can significantly reduce both running costs and energy consumption—while still enjoying a warm, comfortable home.

Improving the energy efficiency of domestic hot-water (DHW) systems usually involves a combination of better heat generation, distribution and demand management. Here are the most effective measures:

1. Upgrade to a high-efficiency heat source  
   • Replace an old electric or oil-fired boiler with a modern condensing gas boiler or an electric heat-pump water heater.  
   • Consider hybrid systems (e.g. gas backup plus heat pump) if your climate has cold extremes.  

2. Insulate storage and distribution  
   • Fit your hot-water tank with a 50–100 mm insulating jacket if it isn’t factory-insulated.  
   • Insulate all hot-water pipes (50 mm or more), especially in unheated spaces (attics, crawl spaces, garages).  

3. Reduce heat losses in the network  
   • Shorten pipe runs and avoid long branch circuits where possible.  
   • Install point-of-use heaters (small electric units) near distant fixtures to avoid running long hot-water lines.  
   • Use thermostatically controlled recirculation loops or on-demand recirculation pumps rather than a continuously circulating system.  

4. Lower the required delivery temperature  
   • Set your water-heater thermostat to 55 – 60 °C (140 – 150 °F) rather than the typical 65 – 70 °C; this reduces standby losses and scald risk when combined with a mixer tap.  
   • Fit thermostatic mixing valves at outlets to deliver 38 – 45 °C while keeping storage at anti-legionella temperature.  

5. Match system capacity to actual demand  
   • Right-size your tank and heat-pump capacity to your household’s peak DHW load rather than oversizing “just in case.”  
   • Install flow-restricting aerators and low-flow showerheads to cut water—and hence heating—volumes by 20–30 %.  

6. Harvest renewable heat  
   • Integrate solar thermal collectors: even a small roof-mounted array can meet 30–60 % of annual DHW needs in many climates.  
   • If you have an air-source or ground-source heat pump for space heating, use its waste heat or defrost cycle heat recovery to preheat DHW.  

7. Control and maintenance  
   • Use timer or smart controls to only heat water during off-peak electricity hours or when solar PV production is high.  
   • Service the system annually—flush sediment from tanks, check anode rods, test thermostats and valves—to maintain optimum performance.  

By combining better insulation, more efficient heat production, reduced distribution losses and smarter controls you can typically cut DHW energy use by 30 – 60 % compared to an older, uninsulated electric or oil-fired system.

Optimizing domestic hot-water (DHW) production in an apartment building involves reducing both the energy required to heat the water and the distribution losses that occur between the plant room and each tap. Below are several strategies—technical, control-based and organizational—you can combine to achieve significant savings.

1. High-efficiency heat generation  
  • Condensing boilers or high-performance heat pumps  
    – Condensing gas boilers or oil boilers can reach efficiencies above 95 % by recovering latent heat from flue gases.  
    – Electric or gas-driven heat pumps (air-source or ground-source) typically achieve coefficients of performance (COPs) of 3–5, greatly reducing electrical input.  
  • Integration with district heating or combined heat‐and‐power (CHP)  
    – If district heating is available, central DHW production can be very efficient.  
    – A small CHP unit supplying both electricity and DHW can further improve total energy yield.  

2. Pre-heating with renewables  
  • Solar thermal collectors  
    – Install solar collectors on the roof to pre-heat the storage tank. In summer months, solar can cover a large share of DHW demand.  
  • Waste heat recovery  
    – Recover heat from building exhaust air (in a central ventilation system) or from greywater (shower drains) and transfer it into the DHW loop via plate heat exchangers.  

3. Storage and distribution losses  
  • Well-insulated storage tanks  
    – Use tanks with high-quality polyurethane or vacuum insulation to limit standby losses to below 1 kWh per m² of tank surface per day.  
  • Minimize pipe run lengths  
    – Group risers vertically and keep horizontal mains short.  
    – Route distribution mains through heated spaces rather than unconditioned attics or crawlspaces.  
  • Pipe insulation and low-loss fittings  
    – Insulate all hot water pipes to at least 25 mm thickness (or in accordance with local code).  
    – Use low-loss, tight-seal mixing valves and fittings to eliminate water dripping and heat losses at points of use.  
  • Controlled recirculation loops  
    – If a recirculation loop is needed, install a temperature‐controlled or timer‐controlled pump so it only runs when there is DHW demand.  
    – Consider thermostatic end-point valves or occupancy sensors that open the pump only when a tap is activated.  

4. Temperature set-points and control  
  • Lower tank temperature within safe limits  
    – Reducing storage temperature from 60 °C to 55 °C can cut standby losses by more than 10 %. Ensure you still meet legionella mitigation requirements (e.g., weekly boost cycles).  
  • Smart control and monitoring  
    – Install flow meters and temperature sensors on major risers to monitor real consumption patterns.  
    – Use building management system (BMS) or smart thermostats to optimize DHW production times (e.g., pump and burner only when forecasts show demand).  
  • Demand-driven operation  
    – For large buildings, zoned DHW systems (one tank per stairwell or per floor) can be switched on only when occupants call for hot water in that zone.  

5. Decentralized or point-of-use solutions  
  • Instantaneous water heaters  
    – In some cases, small electric or gas on-demand units installed under sinks can eliminate long distribution pipe runs altogether.  
  • Booster heaters  
    – If primary production is done at moderate temperature (e.g. 50 °C), local boosters can raise water to desired tap temperature right at the draw-off point, reducing central storage losses.  

6. Preventive maintenance and user engagement  
  • Regular inspection of pumps, valves and heat exchangers ensures the system is operating at design efficiency.  
  • Educate residents on water-saving habits (shorter showers, flow-restricted fixtures) to reduce overall DHW load.  

By combining high‐efficiency generation, renewable pre-heating, tight thermal insulation, smart controls and, where appropriate, decentralized units, you can reduce DHW energy use by 20–50 % compared to a conventional central boiler system. This not only lowers operating costs but also improves comfort and helps meet energy-performance requirements under national regulations and energy‐performance certificates (EPC).

An energy declaration (in Swedish “energideklaration”) is an official certificate that assesses and documents a building’s energy performance. In Sweden it is mandatory to have a valid energy declaration when you sell, rent out or construct a building. Key points:

1. Purpose  
   • Shows how much energy the building uses per square meter and assigns an energy class (A–G) so that buyers or tenants can compare buildings.  
   • Recommends cost-effective measures to reduce energy consumption and operating costs.  

2. Contents  
   • Building type (e.g. detached house, apartment block) – in the register: epc_egenbyggnadstyp  
   • Heated floor area (Atemp) in m² – epc_egenatemp  
   • Number of above-ground floors – epc_egenantalplan  
   • Number of stairwells – epc_egenantaltrapphus  
   • Energy use in kWh/m²·year and resulting energy class – epc_egienergiklass  
   • Description of heating, ventilation, cooling and lighting systems  

3. Process and validity  
   • Performed by an accredited energy expert who inspects the building and its technical installations.  
   • The declaration is registered nationally (linked via Building ID, UUID and EPC address ID) and remains valid for ten years.  
   • If multiple declarations exist, the most recently issued one is the legally valid document.

Energy‐efficiency improvement refers to any changes or upgrades made to a building (or its systems) that reduce the amount of energy required to provide the same level of service—whether that’s heating, cooling, lighting or running appliances. In practice, such improvements can include:

• Building envelope upgrades  
  – Adding or enhancing insulation in walls, roofs and floors  
  – Replacing single-glazed windows with high-performance double or triple glazing  
  – Sealing air leaks around doors, windows and service penetrations  

• Technical system upgrades  
  – Installing high-efficiency boilers, heat pumps or furnaces  
  – Upgrading to more efficient ventilation systems (e.g., heat-recovery ventilators)  
  – Replacing old lighting with LEDs or other low-energy fixtures  

• Control and automation measures  
  – Adding programmable thermostats or building-management systems (BMS) for optimized HVAC operation  
  – Installing occupancy sensors and daylight harvesting controls for lighting  

• Behavioral and operational changes  
  – Educating occupants on energy-saving practices (e.g., thermostat setbacks, switching off unused equipment)  
  – Implementing energy-management routines, such as regular maintenance of heating and cooling equipment  

Benefits of energy‐efficiency improvements  
• Lower energy bills through reduced consumption  
• Improved thermal comfort and indoor air quality  
• Extended service life of building equipment  
• Reduced greenhouse‐gas emissions and environmental impact  

When a building’s energy‐efficiency measures are audited and documented (for example in an Energy Performance Certificate, EPC), the resulting improvement is reflected in a better energy class or score on that certificate.

Properties can contain a variety of premise types—each with its own patterns of occupancy, equipment use and building‐service requirements—and these differences have a direct impact on total energy consumption.  In the context of Sweden’s energy performance certificates (EPCs), premises are generally grouped into two broad categories: residential and non-residential.  Below you’ll find the most common subtypes and a summary of how each affects energy use.  

1. Residential premises  
   • Detached houses, semi-detached (row) houses, terraced houses  
     – Typically have a relatively large envelope area (walls and roof) per unit of floor area, which can increase heating losses.  
     – Occupancy patterns are variable; evenings and weekends tend to see peak heating and hot-water demand.  
   • Apartment blocks (multi-family housing)  
     – Shared walls and floors reduce heat losses on the perimeter, often leading to a lower specific demand for space heating per m².  
     – Centralized heating and hot-water systems can be more efficient, but communal corridors and stairwells require additional ventilation and lighting.  
   • Holiday homes and second‐homes  
     – Intermittent use leads to wide temperature swings; if the house is kept cold most of the year, more energy is used for reheating when occupied.  

2. Non-residential premises  
   • Offices  
     – Moderate heating loads but significant electricity consumption for lighting, computers, servers and other office equipment.  
     – Weekday daytime operation drives clear peaks; efficient control of lighting and HVAC (heating, ventilation and air-conditioning) is critical.  
   • Retail and service premises (shops, restaurants, cafés)  
     – High lighting loads (display lighting, signage) and refrigeration equipment in food outlets.  
     – Extended opening hours—often evenings and weekends—increase the base electrical load.  
   • Industrial and warehouse buildings  
     – Warehouses have large volumes and often minimal insulation, so heating can be costly if the space is conditioned.  
     – Production facilities may have process heat or heavy machinery, which adds to overall energy demand but may also generate recoverable waste heat.  
   • Public and institutional buildings (schools, hospitals, sports halls)  
     – Highly variable occupancy and strict indoor‐climate requirements (ventilation rates, temperature, humidity) can drive up both heating and cooling energy.  
     – Specialized equipment (medical machines, lab equipment, sports‐hall lighting) adds to the electrical load.  

How premise type affects energy consumption  
• Occupancy patterns:  Continuous operation (hospitals) versus intermittent use (homes, holiday houses) dictates heating schedules and standby losses.  
• Internal heat gains:  Computers, lighting and industrial processes can offset some heating demand in winter but increase cooling loads in summer.  
• Building-service systems:  Centralized versus decentralized heating, ventilation strategies (natural vs. mechanical), and the presence of heat recovery all shift the balance between heating, cooling and fan/pump energy.  
• Envelope and geometry:  Compact buildings (apartments) lose less heat per square meter of floor area than sprawling single-family homes or warehouses with high ceilings.  

When commissioning an EPC, the “egenbyggnadstyp” (own building type) and corresponding usage profile are key inputs—together with heated floor area (“Atemp”), number of floors and stairwells—to calculate realistic energy demands and identify the most cost-effective efficiency improvements.

In multifamily or mixed-use buildings, electricity in the shared (common) areas typically serves four main functions:

1. Lighting  
   • General illumination in corridors, lobbies and stairwells, often on time-clocks or motion detectors to minimize waste  
   • Emergency and safety lighting (exit signs, backup luminaires) tied into the fire‐alarm/backup generator  
   • Accent or decorative lighting in reception or lounge areas  

2. Vertical transport and doors  
   • Elevator/moving-walk motor drives and control electronics  
   • Lighting and ventilation inside the lift car  
   • Automated door operators at main entrances or fire egress doors  

3. Ventilation, smoke control and fire safety  
   • Corridor and shaft extract fans or pressurization systems to prevent smoke spread  
   • Stairwell pressurization fans (where required by code)  
   • Power to fire‐alarm control panels, smoke detectors and call‐points  

4. Security, communications and auxiliary services  
   • Access‐control readers, intercoms, CCTV cameras and door‐entry phone systems  
   • Digital signage, directory boards or building‐management SMS/email gateways  
   • Receptacles for cleaning equipment charging or temporary maintenance tools  

In practice these loads are separated onto dedicated sub‐circuits or submeters so that energy‐use in the common areas can be billed or recovered through the building’s operating charges. Timers, presence detectors and building‐management systems are also widely used to optimize run-times and reduce standby waste.

Apartment buildings typically combine a range of measures—both on the building envelope and technical installations—to improve energy performance, reduce operating costs and raise their EPC (energy-efficiency class). Commonly implemented measures include:  

1.  Building-envelope upgrades  
    •  Wall insulation – adding external or cavity insulation to reduce heat loss.  
    •  Loft/roof insulation – upgrading or overlaying existing insulation to minimise heat escaping upwards.  
    •  Floor insulation – insulating over unheated basements or over ground-level slabs.  
    •  High-performance windows and doors – installing double- or triple-glazed units with low-emissivity coatings and well-sealed frames.  

2.  Ventilation and air-tightness  
    •  Mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR) – recovers up to 90 % of the heat in outgoing air and supplies fresh, filtered air.  
    •  Air-tightness improvements – sealing gaps around window frames, pipe penetrations and service ducts to reduce uncontrolled draughts.  

3.  Heating and hot water systems  
    •  Energy-efficient boilers – replacing old, non-condensing boilers with modern condensing gas or biomass boilers.  
    •  Heat pumps – air-source or ground-source heat pumps for space heating and domestic hot water.  
    •  District heating connections – utilising more efficient centralised heat production when available.  
    •  Solar thermal collectors – pre-heating domestic hot water and reducing boiler run times.  

4.  Renewable and on-site generation  
    •  Photovoltaic (PV) panels – generating electricity on-site, often combined with battery storage or net-metering.  
    •  Building-integrated renewables – such as solar thermal façades or small wind turbines where appropriate.  

5.  Lighting and electrical systems  
    •  LED lighting – in common areas, stairwells and parking facilities, often with motion or daylight sensors.  
    •  Smart metering and sub-metering – giving both property managers and residents real-time feedback on electricity, heating and water use.  
    •  Energy-efficient communal equipment – such as modern lift drives, pumps and circulation fans fitted with frequency converters.  

6.  Controls and building automation  
    •  Weather-compensated and time-programmed control of heating systems.  
    •  Individual room thermostats and thermostatic radiator valves – to avoid overheating and allow tenants to set their own comfort levels.

Natural (also called passive) ventilation uses natural forces—wind pressure and thermal buoyancy—to move fresh air through a building, whereas mechanical (active) ventilation relies on powered fans and ductwork. Compared with mechanical systems, natural ventilation offers several advantages:

1. Lower energy consumption  
   • No or very limited fan operation reduces electricity use.  
   • Eliminates energy losses associated with duct leakage and fan heat gain.  

2. Reduced operating and maintenance costs  
   • Fewer moving parts means minimal maintenance (no filters, motors or complex controls).  
   • Lower lifetime costs for repairs and replacement.  

3. Improved indoor comfort and air quality (in suitable climates)  
   • Provides natural airflow patterns that occupants often perceive as more pleasant.  
   • Intro duces outdoor air with natural temperature and humidity fluctuations, which can enhance comfort when conditions are moderate.  

4. Simpler system design and installation  
   • Requires only openings—such as windows, vents or atria—rather than duct networks and mechanical rooms.  
   • Faster to install, with fewer specialized components.  

5. Environmental and sustainability benefits  
   • Eliminates refrigerants and lubricants used in mechanical systems.  
   • Reduces carbon footprint by minimizing electricity demand.  

6. Resilience and robustness  
   • No dependence on mechanical equipment or power supply to maintain air exchange (important during power outages).  
   • Fewer failure points—ventilation continues as long as wind and temperature differences exist.  

Key considerations:  
• Natural ventilation works best in temperate climates or transitional seasons.  
• Performance depends on building orientation, design of openings, prevailing wind conditions and stack effect.  
• In very hot, cold or polluted environments, mechanical ventilation with heat recovery and filtration may be required to achieve comfort, energy efficiency and indoor‐air quality targets.

Optimizing natural ventilation in a house involves careful attention to building orientation, window and opening design, and the way air pathways are managed internally. Even without detailed building-specific data, the following strategies will help you maximize airflow, reduce overheating and indoor pollutants, and improve thermal comfort:

1. Orientation and Layout  
   • Align the long axis of the building perpendicular to prevailing winds. This maximizes cross-ventilation.  
   • Place living spaces (bedrooms, living room) on the windward and leeward sides so air can flow straight through.  
   • Group service areas (bathrooms, closets) in the middle; they act as buffers and don’t require as much fresh air.

2. Window and Opening Design  
   • Use operable windows on opposite walls or at different heights. Large, low openings on the windward side and smaller, high openings on the leeward side induce airflow via pressure differences.  
   • Install trickle vents or adjustable air inlets (for example at head height) to allow a controlled minimum airflow even when windows are closed.  
   • Consider windows with venting flaps or top-hung vents that can remain open in light rain.

3. Exploiting the Stack Effect  
   • Create vertical air paths by placing high-level vents, rooflights or “stack” chimneys in hallways or stairwells. As warm indoor air rises, it exits through these high points and draws cooler air in at low-level openings.  
   • In multi-storey buildings, align vents and shafts through the full height to maximize this buoyancy-driven flow.

4. Pressure and Wind Management  
   • Use simple wind catchers or fixed louvers on the windward façade to funnel breezes indoors, even in low-wind conditions.  
   • Avoid large, uninterrupted solid façades on the leeward side; provide adjustable openings to regulate exit flow and avoid creating excessive back-pressure.

5. Internal Air Pathways  
   • Keep internal doors open or install transfer grilles at the top or bottom of doors so fresh air can move from room to room.  
   • Avoid obstructing corridors and hallways with furniture or full-height partitions that block airflow.

6. Shading and Thermal Mass  
   • Use external shading (eaves, pergolas, trellises) to prevent overheating and reduce the indoor temperature differential—this helps maintain driving forces for ventilative cooling.  
   • Incorporate exposed thermal mass (concrete or tiled floors, masonry walls) so that daytime heat is absorbed and released at night when cooler air is available.

7. Seasonal Tuning  
   • In summer, promote maximum night-time purge ventilation—open as many vents as practical after sunset to cool the building’s thermal mass.  
   • In shoulder seasons, restrict vents to maintain comfortable temperatures while still allowing air exchange to control humidity and pollutants.

8. Maintenance and Operation  
   • Keep vents, louvers and insect screens clean so airflow isn’t impeded by dust or debris.  
   • Educate occupants on how to adjust openings seasonally and in response to wind direction and strength.

By combining proper orientation, well-placed and sized openings, vertical shafts for stack effect, internal air pathways and shading strategies, you can significantly improve natural ventilation performance—lowering reliance on mechanical cooling or ventilation while enhancing indoor comfort and air quality.

The energy class of a building is simply a summary of its overall energy performance—how much energy it requires for heating, cooling, ventilation and domestic hot water. From an appliance-selection standpoint, the building’s energy class affects your decisions in two main ways:

1. Baseline energy demand and cost pressures  
   • A lower (worse) energy class means higher heat losses through walls, roof and windows. That drives up heating costs and makes every extra kilowatt–hour you consume inside the home more expensive in the total energy budget.  
   • A higher (better) energy class means the building envelope is tighter and better insulated. In this case your heating and cooling loads are smaller, so the marginal benefit of an ultra-efficient refrigerator or washing machine still exists—but in relative terms each appliance accounts for a larger share of your total electricity use.

2. Appliance efficiency priorities  
   • In a poorly performing building (e.g. energy class D–G) you will likely see your biggest savings by upgrading the building envelope itself—insulation, windows, ventilation heat recovery—before worrying about small percentage gains in appliance efficiency.  
   • In a well-insulated, high-performance building (energy class A–B), heating and cooling are already optimized, so choosing top-tier appliances (A+++, Energy Star, EU label A or B) will yield more noticeable reductions in your electric bills and carbon footprint.  

Practical guidance  
  • Always check the appliance’s official energy label (EU scale from A+++ down to D or G, depending on the product). Look at the annual energy consumption (kWh/year) rather than just the class letter.  
  • Match appliance capacity to household needs—oversized refrigerators and washing machines may carry a good label but will still consume extra power if used below optimal load.  
  • Consider “smart” or “connected” appliances that allow you to run cycles during off-peak hours or when you have surplus solar generation.  
  • For space heating and cooling, selecting a high-COP heat pump (with a good energy label) can be especially valuable in a high-performance building, where the heat pump runs less often and delivers more of its energy as useful heating or cooling.  
  • In lower-class buildings, prioritize measures that reduce heating demand first (insulation, sealing, ventilation recovery). Once you’ve improved the building’s energy class, focus on upgrading to the most efficient household appliances to maximize your overall savings.  

By understanding your building’s energy class you can strike the right balance between investing in the envelope and selecting appliances with the best energy labels—thereby achieving the lowest total energy costs and environmental impact.

To estimate the total (peak) power demand in your home, you need to inventory every electrical load, determine its rated power and expected simultaneous use, then add them up.  Here’s a step-by-step procedure:

1. Inventory all electrical loads  
   • Lighting (indoor/outdoor fixtures, bulbs)  
   • Appliances (refrigerator, oven, dishwasher, washing machine, dryer, etc.)  
   • HVAC and ventilation (heat pump, boiler circulator pumps, fans)  
   • Small loads (TVs, computers, chargers)  
   • Special equipment (electric vehicle charger, sauna heater, workshop tools)

2. Record each device’s rated power  
   • Look at the nameplate or user manual for wattage (W) or amperage (A) at 230 V  
   • If only current (I) is given, calculate P = V × I (for a single-phase home V ≈ 230 V)

3. Estimate simultaneous‐use (diversity) factors  
   • Not every device runs at full power all the time—for example:  
     – Washing machine/dryer: assume 50–75 % diversity  
     – Lighting: assume 80–100 % of installed wattage if you turn on most lights at once  
     – Refrigerator/compressor loads: often have a diversity factor around 40–50 %  
   • National or local wiring standards often specify diversity tables—consult your electrician or standards (e.g. IEC, SS-EN 60364)

4. Calculate each circuit’s demand  
   • Multiply each device’s rated power by its diversity factor  
   • Sum all adjusted loads on each branch circuit  
   • Check that no branch exceeds its breaker rating (continuous loads ≤ 80 % of breaker capacity)

5. Sum branch demands for total peak power  
   • Add together the highest‐demand circuits (or use an overall diversity rule if allowed)  
   • The result is your estimated maximum power draw in watts or kilowatts

6. Validate or refine with measurement (optional)  
   • Use a clamp ammeter or smart meter to record your actual peak current draw on the main service line  
   • Compare measured peaks to your calculated estimate and adjust diversity factors if necessary

Example (simplified):  
– Lighting total installed: 1 200 W × 0.8 = 960 W  
– Refrigerator: 200 W × 0.5 = 100 W  
– Electric oven: 3 500 W × 1.0 = 3 500 W  
– Washer/dryer: 2 400 W × 0.6 = 1 440 W  
– Miscellaneous (TV, chargers, etc.): 800 W × 0.9 = 720 W  
Total peak demand ≈ 960 + 100 + 3 500 + 1 440 + 720 = 6 720 W (6.7 kW)

Once you have the peak power demand, you can:  
– Size your main fuse or service cable (e.g. a 32 A fuse at 230 V delivers up to 7.4 kW continuous)  
– Specify generator or inverter capacity for backup power  
– Design a photovoltaic or battery storage system to match your load profile

Your total electricity bill is made up of several components, each of which is directly tied to how much electricity you use—and when you use it. Here’s how your consumption affects your price:

1. Variable energy cost (price per kWh)  
   • Most suppliers sell you electricity at a variable “spot” price from the Nord Pool power market. This price changes hour by hour based on supply and demand.  
   • Your actual cost = spot price + supplier’s margin (often a fixed öre/kWh).  
   • The more kilowatt-hours (kWh) you consume, the more you multiply that per-kWh rate.

2. Grid (network) fees  
   • Charged by your local network operator for delivering power to your home.  
   • Usually consists of a fixed monthly fee plus a variable component (öre per kWh).  
   • Higher consumption means a larger variable fee.

3. Taxes and government fees  
   • Energy tax (energi­skatt) and VAT (25%) are calculated on your total kWh usage.  
   • If you use more electricity, your base for these taxes grows.

4. Time-of-use or block tariffs (if your contract includes them)  
   • Time-of-use: You pay different per-kWh rates for “peak” versus “off-peak” hours. Using more power during peak times costs you more.  
   • Block (tiered) tariff: Some contracts lower the per-kWh price once your monthly usage exceeds a certain threshold—so very high consumption may unlock a small volume discount.

5. Demand charges (in some contracts)  
   • A few residential contracts include a fee based on your highest instantaneous power draw (kW).  
   • Large spikes in usage (e.g. starting multiple heavy appliances at once) can increase this component.

Practical takeaway  
– Every extra kWh you draw multiplies the sum of your energy cost, network fee and taxes.  
– Shifting consumption to cheaper hours (if you have time-of-use pricing) can lower your average cost per kWh.  
– Reducing overall consumption (through efficiency measures or behaviour changes) directly reduces both the variable charges and the taxes on your bill.

In liberalized electricity markets (as in Sweden and most of Europe), your relationship with the power system is governed by two separate contracts:

1. Grid (Network) Contract  
   • Who you sign with: the local distribution system operator (DSO), often called the “grid owner” or “grid company.”  
   • What it covers:  
     – Physical transport of electricity from the transmission network to your meter.  
     – Capacity reservation (often expressed as a maximum fuse size or amperage).  
     – Maintenance of cables, transformers and substations up to your property boundary.  
     – Reading or remote-reading of your meter.  
   • Fees and charges:  
     – A fixed monthly fee for connection and administration.  
     – A volumetric fee per kilowatt-hour (kWh) transported.  
     – Possible capacity or peak-load charges if you draw large amounts of power.

2. Electricity Supply (Energy) Contract  
   • Who you sign with: an electricity retailer or supplier (sometimes called an energy trader).  
   • What it covers:  
     – Purchase of the actual electricity you consume.  
     – Choice of contract type (fixed price, variable/dynamic price linked to spot market, green-energy guarantee, etc.).  
     – Any additional services such as green certificates, bundled billing or smart-meter analytics.  
   • Fees and charges:  
     – The commodity price per kWh (fixed or indexed).  
     – Supplier’s markup, retail margin and any environmental or renewable-energy surcharges.  
     – Occasionally a small administration fee.

Why two contracts?  
– Unbundling regulations require that network operation (a natural monopoly) be kept separate from electricity trading (a competitive market).  
– This separation ensures non-discriminatory grid access for all suppliers and clear transparency in what you pay for transport versus the energy itself.

Key takeaway  
You cannot supply yourself with electricity without using someone’s grid—and you cannot use the grid unless you have someone supplying you energy. By maintaining two contracts, you guarantee both a reliable physical connection and competitive choice over the price and origin of the electricity you consume.

Control and regulation technology (sometimes called “automation technology” or “regulation engineering”) is the branch of engineering that deals with measuring, monitoring and automatically adjusting a process or system so that it operates within desired parameters. In the context of building services and industrial processes, it typically comprises:

• Sensors and transducers: devices that measure physical variables (temperature, pressure, flow, humidity, CO₂ concentration, etc.) and convert them into electrical signals.  
• Controllers: hardware or software units (for example PLCs, DDC-controllers or building management systems) that compare measured values against set-points and calculate the corrective action.  
• Actuators and control elements: valves, dampers, pumps, motors or other devices that physically effect changes in the process (e.g. open/close a heating valve, adjust fan speed, dim lighting).  
• Control algorithms and regulation loops: the mathematical logic (PID control, cascade control, predictive control, etc.) that determines how the controller reacts when measurements deviate from set-points.  
• Communication networks and user interfaces: protocols (e.g. Modbus, BACnet, KNX) and software tools that allow operators to visualize system status, change set-points, receive alarms and optimize performance.

By continuously measuring key variables, comparing them to targets and feeding back corrective signals, control and regulation technology ensures systems run safely, efficiently and with minimal manual intervention. In buildings this is critical for indoor climate control (HVAC), lighting and energy optimization; in industry it underpins everything from chemical reactors to conveyor‐belt speed control.

Expanding a building or industrial control system is largely a matter of systematically adding new hardware, software and communication layers while preserving reliability, performance and security. Here is a step-by-step approach:

1. Define your objectives  
   • Identify which additional functions you need (e.g. more temperature or flow control loops, lighting, access control, energy metering).  
   • Quantify the performance requirements (sampling rate, response time, data volume).

2. Choose a scalable architecture  
   • Modular controller platforms (PLCs, DDCs or PACs) that allow you to snap on additional I/O modules.  
   • A hierarchical network design: field level (sensors/actuators), controller level, supervisory (SCADA or building management), and enterprise/IT level.

3. Standardize communication  
   • Adopt open, industry-wide protocols (BACnet/IP, Modbus TCP, KNX, LonWorks, OPC UA) so new devices from different vendors integrate smoothly.  
   • Use managed switches or routers with VLANs to segregate traffic (control vs. office vs. guest network).

4. Provision additional I/O and devices  
   • Plan the physical I/O expansion (digital inputs/outputs, analog channels, Modbus/serial nodes).  
   • Where cabling is expensive or impractical, consider wireless fieldbus (e.g. ISA-100, WirelessHART or Zigbee for low-power sensors).

5. Update or extend the supervisory layer  
   • Add new SCADA/BMS dashboards and database tags to monitor and control the added points.  
   • Ensure your historian or trend-logging system can handle the increased data rate and storage requirements.

6. Implement data integration and analytics  
   • If you need enterprise-level reporting or energy optimization, integrate your control system with an IoT or cloud platform via REST/APIs or MQTT.  
   • Apply analytics and machine-learning tools to identify inefficiencies or predict maintenance needs.

7. Ensure cybersecurity and resilience  
   • Protect new network segments with firewalls, access control lists and intrusion detection.  
   • Use VPN tunnels or secure gateways for remote access.  
   • Plan redundancy for critical controllers and communication links (e.g. ring topologies, dual-path cabling).

8. Test, commission and document  
   • Perform factory acceptance tests (FAT) on the new modules.  
   • Conduct site acceptance tests (SAT) and functional testing with all interlocks.  
   • Update your system documentation, network diagrams and operational procedures.

By following this structured, layered approach—scalable controllers, open communications, robust networking and strong cybersecurity—you can reliably expand your control system as needs evolve, without compromising performance or maintainability.

   - Fast (sometimes “accelerated”): 3.7 kW up to 22 kW (three-phase, 400 V)  
   - High-power AC: 22 kW up to 43 kW  

2. DC (direct-current) charging  
   - Semi-fast: 22 kW to 50 kW  
   - Rapid (often simply called “fast” or “ultra-fast”): typically ≥50 kW  
   - Very high-power ultra-fast: 150 kW, 350 kW and above  

Key “boundary” points to remember:  
 • 22 kW (AC) is widely regarded in the EU as the switch from “normal/slow” to “fast” AC charging.  
 • 50 kW (DC) is generally considered the entry point for rapid DC charging capable of 100 km+ of range in 10–20 minutes.  

In North America the terminology often maps to SAE Levels:  
 • Level 1 (120 V AC, up to ~1.9 kW) – very slow  
 • Level 2 (240 V AC, up to ~19.2 kW) – “normal” or “fast” home/work charging  
 • Level 3 (DC fast, ≥50 kW) – rapid public charging  

So, if you’re comparing home or workplace charging infrastructures, anything above ~3.7 kW AC up to ~22 kW AC is usually termed “fast AC.” Public charging stations that deliver DC at 50 kW or more are almost universally called “fast,” “rapid” or “ultra-fast” chargers.

Load balancing for EV charging is a way to manage and distribute the available electrical capacity among multiple charging points so that no circuit or connection is overloaded. By dynamically adjusting how much power each vehicle receives, a load-balancing system:

1. Prevents Overloads  
   • Monitors total current draw in real time  
   • Automatically reduces or increases charging currents to stay within the safe limits of the building’s electrical installation

2. Optimizes Available Capacity  
   • If one charger is idle, others may increase their share of power  
   • In busy charging facilities (e.g. apartment garage or workplace), ensures that every plugged-in vehicle receives a fair portion of the available amperage

3. Reduces Infrastructure Costs  
   • Avoids the need for expensive grid upgrades or higher-capacity mains just to cover peak loads  
   • Uses existing transformers and switchgear more efficiently

4. Improves Energy Efficiency and Flexibility  
   • Can integrate with on-site renewable generation (solar panels) or battery storage  
   • Works with demand-response signals from the grid to charge when electricity is cheapest or cleanest

Types of Load Balancing  
• Static Load Balancing – Allocates a fixed percentage of the total available current to each charger (for example, two chargers each get 50 %).  
• Dynamic (Real-Time) Load Balancing – Continuously measures the building’s total consumption and dynamically adjusts each charger’s output based on current demand and predefined priorities.

Key Components  
• Current Sensors or Energy Meters – Track the total and individual charger loads.  
• Central Controller or Energy Management System – Aggregates measurements, applies balancing logic and issues set-point commands to each charging unit.  
• Communication Protocol (often OCPP) – Allows chargers and the controller to exchange load-management instructions.

Benefits at a Glance  
• Safety: avoids tripped breakers and overloads  
• Cost Savings: postpones or eliminates costly electrical upgrades  
• User Experience: ensures consistent minimum charging speeds for all vehicles  
• Grid Friendliness: smooths peaks, supports integration of renewables and participation in demand-response programs

Recommended light levels for stairwells are governed by both safety and comfort criteria.  In Sweden (and more broadly under European standard EN 12464-1:2011), the following values are generally applied:

1. General (normal) lighting  
   • Maintained illuminance on the walking surface (nosing line of steps): 100 lux  
   • Maintained illuminance on landings: 100 lux  
   • Uniformity (minimum/average): ≥ 0.4  

   – “Maintained illuminance” means the light level expected over time, taking into account lamp depreciation and dirt accumulation.  
   – A uniformity ratio of 0.4 ensures there are no deep shadows, which could obscure a step edge.

2. Emergency (escape‐route) lighting  
   • Minimum illuminance along the escape path at floor level: 1 lux  
   • At safety signage and door handles: 5 lux  

3. Additional recommendations  
   • Highlight the first and last step with accent lighting or contrasting materials.  
   • Use LED fixtures with good color rendering (CRI ≥ 80) to improve depth perception.  
   • Maintain mounting heights and light‐direction to avoid glare or overly bright spots.

By designing for 100 lux maintained lighting and appropriate emergency levels, you ensure that stairwells remain safe, clearly legible and comfortable to use throughout the building’s life cycle.

Improving lighting in basement areas typically involves a combination of maximizing available natural light, selecting the right artificial fixtures, optimizing surface reflectance and using proper controls. Below are several strategies you can apply:

1. Introduce or Enhance Natural Light  
  • Light wells and window wells – If your basement has windows below grade, installing or enlarging window wells with reflective sidewalls and clear covers can bring in more daylight.  
  • Sun tunnels or tubular skylights – Flexible“light pipes” capture roof-level daylight and channel it down into interior spaces. They work well even where traditional windows aren’t possible.

2. Use Layered Artificial Lighting  
  • Ambient lighting – Install evenly spaced LED ceiling fixtures (panels, downlights or linear fixtures) to provide general illumination. Aim for 200–300 lux for circulation and storage areas; higher if the space will be used as living quarters or a workspace.  
  • Task lighting – Over workbenches, laundry areas or desks, add under-cabinet LEDs, adjustable track lights or swing-arm wall lights to achieve 300–500 lux where precision tasks are done.  
  • Accent lighting – If you have architectural features (e.g. exposed brick, shelving), use small spotlights or LED tape to create visual interest and reduce the perception of a “flat” ceiling.

3. Select Energy-Efficient, High-Quality Fixtures  
  • LED technology – Choose LEDs with an efficacy of at least 100 lm/W to minimize energy use.  
  • Color rendering and temperature – Specify a Color Rendering Index (CRI) of 80 or above so colors look natural, and select a color temperature of 3000–4000 K for a warm-but-crisp feel.  
  • Moisture and dust protection – In utility or storage basements, use fixtures rated at least IP44; in damp or utility areas, consider IP65-rated fixtures.

4. Optimize Surface Reflectance  
  • Light-colored walls and ceilings – Bright whites or pale neutrals with a matte or eggshell finish will reflect more light than dark hues.  
  • Reflective floor treatments – Polished concrete or light-tone epoxy coatings can bounce light upward, reducing shadows.

5. Incorporate Controls and Zoning  
  • Dimmers and multiple circuits – Group fixtures into zones so you can tailor light levels to specific activities and avoid over-lighting.  
  • Occupancy/vacancy sensors – In seldom-used storage or mechanical rooms, sensors automatically switch lights on and off, saving energy.  
  • Daylight harvesting – Where natural light is present, use photocell controls to dim or turn off artificial lighting when daylight is sufficient.

6. Plan for Maintenance and Safety  
  • Accessible fixtures – Choose recessed or surface-mounted designs that allow easy lamp or driver replacement.  
  • Emergency lighting and egress – In habitable basements, code may require emergency-backup luminaires or illuminated exit signage. Ensure corridors and stairs meet minimum lux requirements for safe evacuation.

By combining these approaches—bringing in daylight where possible, layering efficient artificial light, maximizing reflectance, and employing smart controls—you can transform a dark, dingy basement into a bright, comfortable and functional space.

  – At this level you ensure reasonable comfort and safe, slip-free evacuation in winter conditions.  

Note that there is no “one size fits all” value – the exact set-point can be adjusted depending on the building’s insulation, climate zone and energy strategy – but under no circumstances should the temperature drop below roughly 10 °C.

1. Assess current performance  
   • Obtain or update an Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) to establish your building’s current energy class and pinpoint main sources of heat loss.  
   • Review your annual energy bills and, if possible, carry out a basic thermographic survey or blower-door test to identify leaks.

2. Building envelope upgrades  
   • Roof/attic insulation – often the single most cost-effective measure, since heat rises and insulation pays back quickly.  
   • Wall insulation – internal or external, especially for uninsulated or poorly insulated masonry or timber walls.  
   • Floor and basement insulation – to reduce heat loss to the ground, particularly in older buildings with suspended timber or uninsulated slabs.  
   • Airtightness improvement – seal gaps around windows, doors and service penetrations, then introduce controlled ventilation.

3. High-performance windows and doors  
   • Replace single-glazed or old double-glazed units with modern, low-U-value glazing.  
   • Ensure frames are thermally broken and properly sealed.

4. Ventilation and indoor climate control  
   • Install mechanical ventilation with heat recovery (MVHR) to supply fresh air while recouping heat from stale exhaust air.  
   • Service and balance existing systems; add demand-controlled ventilation (humidity or CO₂ sensors) where feasible.

5. Heating and hot water systems  
   • Upgrade to a high-efficiency boiler or heat pump (air-source or ground-source) sized correctly for your building’s reduced heat demand.  
   • Fit smart controls and thermostatic radiator valves so you heat only when and where you need it.  
   • Insulate hot water tanks and distribution pipes to minimise standby losses.

6. Lighting and electrical systems  
   • Replace old lamps with LEDs and fit presence or daylight sensors in corridors, stairwells and offices.  
   • Review major electrical appliances (elevators, kitchen equipment, pumps) for efficiency ratings and operating schedules.

7. On-site renewable energy  
   • Once demand is reduced, consider photovoltaics (PV) on suitable roof surfaces or small-scale wind or solar thermal systems to offset grid electricity and water heating.

8. Monitoring and maintenance  
   • Install sub-metering or an energy-management system to track performance of individual systems.  
   • Regularly service HVAC equipment, clean filters and check insulation integrity.

By following this sequence—envelope first, then systems, then renewables—you will achieve the greatest energy savings for the lowest upfront cost and improve your EPC energy class over time.

   • Rooftop solar photovoltaics (PV) to offset electricity consumption.

Reducing standby (or “vampire”) electricity consumption in shared areas such as lounges, kitchens, conference rooms and corridors is both cost-effective and environmentally responsible. Below are practical steps you can implement:

1. Equip and Organize  
   • Use switched power strips or smart outlets  
     – Install strips with master-slave functionality so that when the primary device (e.g. a conference‐room PC) is turned off, peripheral equipment (printer, speakers, chargers) also powers down.  
     – Consider smart plugs that can be scheduled or controlled centrally via a building management system (BMS).  
   • Group devices logically  
     – Cluster TVs, audio systems, coffee machines and vending machines on dedicated circuits or strips. This makes it easier for staff to switch them all off at once.

2. Automate Shutdowns  
   • Schedule automatic power-off  
     – Use timers or BMS rules so that non-critical equipment in meeting rooms and break areas shuts down after hours or during known idle periods (e.g. nights and weekends).  
   • Motion or occupancy sensors  
     – In corridors and medium-use lounges, install sensors that cut power to lighting and low-power devices when nobody is present.

3. Policy and Training  
   • End-of-day procedure  
     – Define clear responsibilities (e.g. last person out closes down all equipment in shared spaces).  
     – Post simple checklists on or near power panels, reminding staff to switch off.  
   • Awareness campaigns  
     – Share data on energy savings achieved by reducing standby losses.  
     – Use signage (“Did you switch me off?”) near frequently overlooked devices—coffee makers, water dispensers, phone‐charging stations.

4. Equipment Selection and Maintenance  
   • Choose low-standby appliances  
     – When replacing or purchasing new shared‐use devices, specify models with <1 W standby draw and ENERGY STAR or EU EcoDesign certification.  
   • Regular audits  
     – Periodically measure standby consumption with portable meters. Identify “energy vampires” and retire or upgrade them.

5. Monitoring and Continuous Improvement  
   • Integrate with energy dashboards  
     – Feed real-time data from submeters or smart plugs into a central dashboard to spot unexpected standby loads.  
   • Set targets and review  
     – Establish monthly or quarterly goals for reducing standby consumption (e.g. a 20% reduction in off-hour loads) and report progress to facility managers.

By combining behavioral measures, simple automation and smarter equipment choice, you can cut unnecessary electricity draw in shared spaces by up to 30 % or more—lowering costs and contributing to your building’s overall energy performance.

Before you commit to installing solar panels on a condominium or multi‐unit building, your board should carry out a thorough review in at least the following areas:

   • Confirm that the condominium association’s statutes or by-laws allow rooftop installations—and if necessary secure a board resolution or owner approval.  
   • Investigate any protected‐building (heritage) rules or neighborhood covenants that may restrict solar arrays.  
   • Apply for all necessary local building permits and, where relevant, a grid connection permit from your Distribution System Operator (DSO).

3. Energy performance and economic viability  
   • Consult your latest Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) to understand current energy use (Atemp) and efficiency class—this helps size the PV system and project payback.  
   • Model expected generation against common load profiles in the building to estimate savings.  
   • Explore available grants, tax incentives or net‐metering schemes that reduce upfront cost.

4. Fire, safety and access considerations  
   • Ensure panels and wiring comply with national electrical and fire-safety standards, with clear evacuation and maintenance routes.  
   • Plan for snow and ice shedding, gutter clearance and adequate ventilation beneath panels.

5. Installer qualifications and warranties  
   • Solicit bids from certified solar PV installers with proven track records on multi‐unit buildings.  
   • Check installer liability insurance, valid F-tax status (in Sweden) and ask for references.  
   • Secure manufacturer’s warranties on modules, inverters and mounting systems—and a workmanship guarantee from the installer.

6. Insurance and long-term maintenance  
   • Inform your property insurer about the installation and update coverage for potential fire, storm or hail damage.  
   • Agree a maintenance and cleaning schedule (e.g., annual checks of fixings, electrical connections and panel cleanliness).

An apartment building can typically reduce its domestic hot-water energy use through a combination of system upgrades, better insulation and controls, low-flow fixtures, and heat-recovery measures.  Below are the most effective strategies:

1. Optimize the Central Hot-Water System  
   • Insulate storage tanks and all hot-water distribution piping (including risers and recirculation loops) to minimize standby losses.  
   • Install variable‐speed recirculation pumps controlled by thermostats or timers so water is only circulated when needed.  
   • Lower the standard set-point temperature to the minimum acceptable level (e.g. from 60 °C to 55 °C) while retaining a periodic “legionella‐flush” at higher temperature.  

2. Upgrade to Efficient Heat Generators  
   • Replace old electric boilers or direct‐fired units with high-efficiency condensing boiler(s) or, ideally, a water-heater heat pump.  
   • Consider a centralized heat‐pump hot‐water system (air-to-water or ground-source) which can cut energy consumption by 50–70 % compared to electric resistance.  
   • In cold‐climate or district-heating areas, upgrade to a modern condensing connection that recovers heat from return water.  

3. Recover Heat from Wastewater  
   • Install drain‐water heat-recovery units (e.g. shell‐and‐tube exchangers or heat‐pipe units) on shower drains. These can pre-heat incoming cold water by 20–30 %.  

4. Fit Low-Flow and Smart Fixtures  
   • Equip all shower heads, faucets and aerators with low-flow versions (e.g. 7 L/min instead of 10–12 L/min).  
   • Use thermostatic mixer valves or electronic taps that shut off automatically if the user walks away.  
   • Promote sensible hot-water habits among residents (shorter showers, only filling the kettle, etc.).  

5. Decentralized or Point-Of-Use Options  
   • Where riser lengths are very long, consider small point-of-use heat‐pump water heaters in corridors or individual apartments to eliminate distribution losses altogether.  
   • Combine with sub-metering so each household pays directly for its own hot‐water energy, encouraging conservation.  

6. Smart Controls and Monitoring  
   • Deploy sensors and building‐automation controls to track tank temperatures, flow-rates and circulation‐pump energy.  
   • Generate regular reports or dashboards for maintenance staff, and share consumption data with tenants to drive behavior change.  

7. Routine Maintenance  
   • Descale heat exchangers and tanks annually to preserve efficiency.  
   • Check insulation integrity, pump performance and valve operation.  
   • Balance risers and stair-well loops to ensure even temperatures and minimize excessive circulation.  

By combining good insulation, efficient generation (especially heat pumps), waste‐heat recovery, water-saving fixtures and smart controls, an apartment building can typically cut its domestic hot water energy use by 30–60 %.

Ventilation balancing is the process of measuring and adjusting the airflows in a building’s mechanical ventilation system so that each supply-air and extract-air outlet delivers exactly the airflow rate for which it was designed. When done correctly, balancing ensures that

• no rooms are over-ventilated (which wastes energy by heating or cooling more outside air than necessary)  
• no rooms are under-ventilated (which can lead to poor indoor air quality and uneven temperature distribution)  
• the supply and exhaust airflows are equalized, minimizing uncontrolled infiltration and exfiltration through cracks, windows and doors  

Energy-use implications of proper ventilation balancing  
1. Reduced heat losses and gains  
   – In winter, you only heat the exact quantity of fresh air you need, rather than over-ventilating and losing unnecessary heat up the exhaust.  
   – In summer, you avoid bringing in and then air-conditioning excess warm, humid air.  

2. Optimized fan power  
   – Fans run at their design flow and static pressure points, which is more energy-efficient than running them too hard (to overcome leaks or imbalances) or too lightly (where airflow control devices may throttle inefficiently).  

3. Improved performance of heat‐recovery devices  
   – Balanced airflow through heat‐exchange cores (in a heat‐recovery ventilator) maximizes thermal transfer between outgoing and incoming air streams, directly reducing the load on heating and cooling systems.  

4. More predictable overall HVAC load  
   – When ventilation rates are exactly known and controlled, it’s easier to size and run heating and cooling equipment at optimal efficiency, rather than compensating for unexpected infiltration or uneven room temperatures.  

Typical energy savings from a properly balanced system can range from 5 % to 20 % of the building’s HVAC energy use, depending on how poorly the system was performing before balancing and the presence of heat-recovery equipment. In practice, commissioning and periodic re-balancing are recommended to maintain those savings over the life of the building.
